records.our_prose: Open-pollinated, mostly indeterminate tomatoes grown for flavor and diversity. The defining trait of an heirloom is that it is open-pollinated: it breeds true from saved seed, so a Brandywine grown from last year's seed comes back as Brandywine, unlike an F1 hybrid whose saved seed segregates into a mix of the parent traits. Heirlooms span an enormous range of size, color, and shape, from the dusky Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, to the green-when-ripe Green Zebra, to two-pound pink Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, to open-pollinated paste types like San Marzano and Amish Paste. Most classic heirlooms are indeterminate: the vine keeps extending and setting fruit until frost, so it needs strong staking or caging and benefits from pruning to one or two main stems. Days to maturity vary widely by variety, roughly 70 to 90 days from transplant. The main tradeoff is disease: heirlooms generally lack the Verticillium, Fusarium, and nematode resistance (the VFN codes) bred into modern hybrids, so they are more prone to the soilborne wilts, to early and late blight and Septoria leaf spot, and to fruit cracking, and they reward attentive rotation, sanitation, and even watering. Like all tomatoes they need a long frost-free window and set fruit poorly once day temperatures pass the upper 80s°F or nights stay above about 70°F.

records.our_prose: Most heirloom tomatoes are indeterminate: the vine keeps growing and setting fruit until frost and can reach 6 to 8 feet, so it needs sturdy staking or caging and continuous support. Prune to one or two main stems for larger fruit and better airflow, which also helps limit the foliar diseases heirlooms are prone to. A few heirlooms are compact or semi-determinate (the open-pollinated Stupice runs early and bushy; paste types like Amish Paste are often semi-determinate), but the classic large slicers (Brandywine, Cherokee Purple, Mortgage Lifter) are strongly indeterminate.

records.our_prose: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow heirloom on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for heirloom, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

records.our_prose: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow heirloom as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited heirloom sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

records.our_prose: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, and water deeply so it soaks well down. Heirloom roots go quite deep, and deep watering pulls them down where they handle heat and dry spells better; quick shallow sprinkles keep roots near the surface where they dry out fast.

records.source_context: Transplants can be watered overhead, or they may be watered from the bottom. To water transplants from the bottom, simply fill a container or lid with 1 to 2 inches of water and set the transplant tray into the water reservoir. Allow the transplant tray to absorb water for 3 to 10 minutes and place the tray back under the grow lights.

records.our_prose: Keep water off the foliage: overhead irrigation creates the leaf-surface wetness Septoria leaf spot and early blight need to infect. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so foliage dries before nightfall. Mulch to steady soil moisture, which also limits the blossom-end rot that large-fruited types are especially prone to.

records.source_context: If possible, irrigate only the soil using furrows, drip lines, or soaker hoses. If us­ ing overhead (sprinkler) irrigation, do it in the morning so the plants dry quickly as the day warms. Insufficient soil moisture or poor water uptake due to root damage or disease may produce fruits with blossom end rot.

records.our_prose: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95°F, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit; this is heat stress, not a disease. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. Shade cloth draped over the plant during the hottest part of the afternoon can help if you have it.
